variables.claim_asserts: The sutural line of a high-spired shell such as Turritella is a geodesic on its right-conical envelope, with coils tightening toward the apex.
variables.test_measures: For fossil Turritellidae specimens, observed total whorl number divided by the maximum total turns N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)) available to any geodesic on a right cone with the measured apical angle.

modality.note: Per-specimen apical angle and whorl count provide a direct necessary-condition test of the literal conical-geodesic identification; a curve exceeding the cone's global turn bound cannot be that geodesic.

assumptions.note: The analysis adopts Thompson's stated right-cone idealization. Real shells and early whorls depart from it, but subtracting two early whorls still leaves all 34 specimens above the bound.

scope.claim_scope: High-spired gastropod shells, exemplified by Turritella.
scope.test_scope: Thirty-four Neogene West Java specimens from four Turritellidae species with both apical angle and whorl count.

reasons: The ratio R = N_obs/N_geo tests a necessary consequence of the exact object Thompson names: a geodesic on the shell's right-conical envelope.
All 34 specimens have R > 1, ranging from 1.63 to 3.39, so their sutures make more turns than such a conical geodesic can make.
The criterion does not confuse tightening coils with geodesicity; it explicitly leaves the non-discriminating tightening statement untested and bases refutation on the stronger identification.
The fossil West Java sample covers only four species and uses gross apical angles, so it faithfully refutes the literal model for that declared subset rather than all high-spired shells.
what_would_change_it: Trace complete sutural curves and fit specimen-specific shell surfaces for a broad sample including living Turritella and the type species, then calculate geodesic curvature directly; agreement with zero within uncertainty would supersede the conical turn-bound proxy.
